categories: ["สภาพตับและดีซ่าน"]
conventional_description:
Liver fibrosis is the accumulation of scar tissue in the liver in response to chronic injury. Over time, repeated damage from conditions such as hepatitis B or C, heavy alcohol use, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) triggers a wound-healing response that deposits collagen and other matrix proteins. As fibrosis advances, the liver becomes stiffer and its ability to perform vital functions - filtering blood, producing proteins, storing energy - declines.
Early fibrosis often causes no symptoms; as it progresses, patients may experience fatigue, vague right-sided abdominal discomfort, or mild jaundice. Diagnosis typically involves blood tests, imaging (ultrasound, elastography like FibroScan), and sometimes liver biopsy. The key goal of conventional treatment is to stop or slow the underlying cause to prevent progression to cirrhosis.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause: antiviral medications for hepatitis B or C, abstinence from alcohol, weight loss and metabolic control for fatty liver disease. There are currently no FDA-approved anti-fibrotic drugs that directly reverse scarring; management aims to halt progression. In advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, monitoring for complications (varices, ascites, liver cancer) is essential.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, liver fibrosis is understood through the lens of the Liver organ system, which governs the smooth flow of Qi and stores Blood. When this flow is disrupted - by chronic emotional stress, dietary indiscretions, or external pathogens like viruses - Qi stagnates, and over time, this stagnation transforms into Heat, Dampness, and eventually Blood stasis. This progressive congestion in the liver's network of vessels (the collaterals) is what TCM recognizes as the formation of 'accumulations' (积聚) and 'hypochondriac masses' (痞块).
The Spleen plays a critical role because it transforms food into Qi and Blood and manages Dampness. When the Liver is stuck, it overacts on the Spleen, impairing digestion and leading to the accumulation of Dampness and Phlegm. This combination of Qi stagnation and Damp-Heat is especially common in fibrosis driven by alcohol or a rich, fatty diet, manifesting as distending rib pain, bitter taste, and greasy tongue coating.
If the stagnation persists, the Qi congestion begins to affect the Blood. The blood flow slows and congeals, forming fixed, stabbing pain and palpable masses under the ribs. This Blood Stasis pattern is often seen in advanced fibrosis or early cirrhosis, where the tongue turns purplish with dark spots and the pulse becomes choppy.
As the disease progresses and the body's resources are drained, a deficiency pattern emerges. The chronic inflammation and scarring consume both Qi (vital energy) and Yin (moistening fluids), leading to profound fatigue, dry mouth, and a thin, weak pulse. This Qi and Yin Deficiency pattern reflects a state where the liver is no longer being adequately nourished, allowing scarring to continue unchecked.
classical_translation: "When the liver is diseased, there is pain under both ribs that radiates to the lower abdomen."
tcm_diagnosis:
When liver qi is stuck and the spleen is weakened with emerging heat, the discomfort is a distending, moving ache in the rib area that flares with stress or frustration. You may also feel tired, have a poor appetite, and notice loose stools, but with a bitter taste in the mouth and a tendency toward irritability. The tongue often has red edges and a thin yellow coating, while the pulse feels wiry and rapid.
If damp-heat is the dominant pattern, the hypochondriac pain is more intense and accompanied by a greasy bitter taste, nausea, and sometimes yellowing of the skin or eyes. This pattern is especially common when the fibrosis follows viral hepatitis or heavy alcohol use. The tongue appears red with a thick, greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is typically slippery and rapid, reflecting the internal heat and dampness.
Blood stagnation produces a different quality of pain: it is fixed, stabbing, and often associated with a sensation of a lump or firmness under the right ribs. The complexion may look dark or sallow, and the tongue becomes purplish with possible dark spots. The pulse is wiry and choppy, as if the blood is struggling to flow smoothly through the liver's small vessels.
In more advanced stages, qi and yin deficiency leaves the person profoundly drained. The rib pain is dull and lingering, worse after exertion, and is accompanied by dry mouth, night sweats, and a lack of appetite. The tongue is pale with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and weak. This pattern signals that the body's nourishing resources are depleted and repair is sluggish.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation with Spleen Qi Deficiency that transforms into Heat
patterns.symptoms: ["Distending or wandering rib pain", "Worse with emotional stress", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Bloating and loose stools", "Irritability and quick temper", "Fatigue and low energy"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, Fatty or greasy foods, Alcohol consumption, Overwork
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise or stretching, Stress reduction, Warm, easily digestible meals, Adequate rest, Avoiding alcohol
patterns.why_this_happens: When stress and emotional tension persist, Liver Qi stagnates and cannot flow freely. This stagnation weakens the Spleen, impairing digestion and leading to dampness. Over time, the pent-up Qi and dampness generate Heat, which further injures the Liver and Spleen. The combination of Qi stagnation, dampness, and Heat disrupts blood flow in the Liver, contributing to the formation of fibrotic tissue.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, teeth marks, thin to moderately thick yellow and slightly greasy coating. Pulse: wiry (xian) and rapid, especially wiry at the left Guan (Liver) position, possibly weak at the right Guan (Spleen).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly aggravates Liver Qi stagnation, which is the root of this pattern. Greasy foods and alcohol overwhelm the Spleen, creating more dampness and heat that further obstruct the Liver. Gentle movement and stress reduction help Qi flow smoothly, while warm, simple foods strengthen the Spleen and reduce dampness, easing the burden on the Liver.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals that are easy to digest, such as congee and steamed vegetables. Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods that generate dampness and heat. Limit alcohol completely. Practice stress management through gentle movement like tai chi or walking, and ensure adequate rest to support the Spleen.

patterns.why_this_happens: Damp-Heat accumulates in the Liver and Gallbladder, often from alcohol, a rich greasy diet, or a lingering viral infection. The heat and dampness obstruct the flow of Qi and Blood, creating a state of persistent inflammation that damages liver tissue. Over time, this unresolved inflammation and stagnation leads to the formation of scar tissue, which is the fibrosis itself.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red sides and a thick, yellow, greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat thrives on heating and damp-producing inputs like alcohol, greasy food, and stress, which inflame the liver. Cooling, drying foods and rest help drain the dampness and clear the heat, allowing the liver to heal and fibrosis to slow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid alcohol, fried foods, spicy dishes, and heavy meats that create damp-heat. Favor cooling, light foods like mung bean soup, cucumber, bitter gourd, and leafy greens. Stay hydrated with warm water or barley tea, not iced drinks. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi circulate without overheating.

patterns.worse_with: Sedentary lifestyle, Cold weather or drafts, Fatty or greasy foods, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Warm compress on the area, Gentle exercise or stretching, Light, non-greasy meals, Rest in a calm environment
patterns.why_this_happens: Long-standing inflammation and Qi congestion in liver fibrosis eventually slow the blood flow, causing it to congeal in the tiny vessels (collaterals) of the liver. This stagnant blood forms hard, fixed lumps under the ribs and produces a deep, stabbing ache that worsens at night when the body's circulation naturally slows. The dark complexion, purplish lips, and dusky tongue reflect the lack of fresh blood reaching the tissues.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Purple or dusky body with stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coating. Pulse: Choppy (涩 Sè), wiry (弦 Xián) or firm (牢 Láo).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis is like a traffic jam in the liver's tiny vessels. Cold and inactivity thicken the blood and slow its flow, while warmth and gentle movement keep it circulating. Greasy foods create dampness that further clogs the vessels. Emotional stress tightens the Liver Qi, which in turn stagnates blood. Therefore, keeping warm, moving gently, eating cleanly, and managing stress all help to break up the stasis and restore flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat lightly and include blood-moving foods like hawthorn berry (山楂 shān zhā), turmeric, and small amounts of saffron. Avoid greasy, heavy meals that bog down circulation. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi and blood flowing.

patterns.better_with: Adequate rest, Warm, moistening foods (congee, soups), Gentle exercise or stretching, Staying hydrated with warm fluids
patterns.why_this_happens: As liver fibrosis progresses, the chronic illness drains the body’s fundamental energy (Qi) and its nourishing fluids (Yin). When Qi is depleted, you feel profoundly tired and short of breath, while Yin deficiency leaves your mouth and throat dry and fails to moisten the liver, allowing scarring to worsen. The Spleen’s digestive power also weakens, leading to poor appetite and a cycle of deeper fatigue and malnourishment of the liver.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body with little or no coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Rest and gentle movement conserve Qi, while overwork and stress deplete it. Spicy and drying foods consume Yin fluids, worsening dryness and fatigue. Nourishing, moistening foods and adequate sleep help rebuild both Qi and Yin, supporting the body's ability to repair liver tissue.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid overexertion. Eat small, frequent meals of easily digestible, nourishing foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and bone broths. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods that can further deplete Yin fluids. Gentle exercises like Tai Chi or walking can help maintain Qi flow without draining energy.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse liver fibrosis?
faqs.answer: TCM's goal is to halt progression and, in many cases, promote regression of fibrosis by addressing the root imbalance. Studies on herbs like those in Fu Fang Bie Jia Ruan Gan Pian and Fuzheng Huayu capsule have shown anti-fibrotic effects. While results vary, many patients see stabilization and some reversal on imaging after consistent treatment.

faqs.question: How long does it take for herbs to work on liver fibrosis?
faqs.answer: Most patients notice symptom relief within 4-8 weeks, but changes in liver stiffness may take 3-6 months. Chronic fibrosis that has developed over years will not reverse overnight; consistency is key. Your practitioner will monitor progress with regular tongue and pulse assessments, adjusting the formula as needed.

faqs.question: Can I take TCM herbs with my antiviral medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, most Chinese herbs for liver fibrosis can be safely combined with antivirals like tenofovir or entecavir. However, always inform both your hepatologist and TCM practitioner. Some herbs like Da Huang (rhubarb) may affect absorption if taken simultaneously, so spacing doses by at least 2 hours is recommended. Never stop prescribed antivirals without your doctor's guidance.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture effective for liver fibrosis?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture helps regulate Qi flow, reduce inflammation, and improve digestive symptoms. It is a supportive therapy rather than a direct anti-fibrotic, but many patients find it reduces stress, pain, and fatigue, creating a better environment for healing. Points like Taichong LR-3 and Zusanli ST-36 are commonly used to soothe the Liver and strengthen the Spleen.

faqs.question: What dietary changes should I make with liver fibrosis?
faqs.answer: A TCM diet for liver fibrosis emphasizes light, easily digestible foods that avoid burdening the Spleen. Avoid alcohol completely, and limit greasy, fried, and spicy foods that generate Damp-Heat. Favor cooked vegetables, congees, and moderate amounts of lean protein. Cooling foods like mung beans and bitter gourd can be helpful if you have a Damp-Heat pattern.

faqs.question: When should I see a doctor instead of a TCM practitioner?
faqs.answer: TCM can complement but not replace conventional monitoring. If you have new or worsening jaundice, fluid buildup in the abdomen, confusion, or bleeding, seek immediate medical care. For routine monitoring, continue your regular liver specialist visits. See our Safety section below for a full list of urgent symptoms.

research.title: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of hepatic fibrosis with integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine (2019 edition)
research.description: This clinical practice guideline, issued by the Chinese Association of Integrative Medicine, provides evidence-based recommendations for TCM pattern differentiation and herbal therapy in liver fibrosis. It endorses formulas such as Yin Chen Hao Tang for damp-heat, Fuzheng Huayu capsule for qi deficiency and blood stasis, and Biejia Ruangan tablet for blood stasis with spleen-kidney deficiency.
research.periodical: Chinese Association of Integrative Medicine Liver Disease Committee. Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of hepatic fibrosis with integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine (2019 edition). Chinese Journal of Hepatology. 2019.

research.title: Progress on traditional Chinese medicine in improving hepatic fibrosis through inhibiting oxidative stress
research.description: This review summarizes the anti-fibrotic mechanisms of key TCM formulas, including Fuzheng Huayu Fang and Yin Chen Hao Tang, focusing on their ability to attenuate oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokines. It highlights that these multi-herb preparations can halt the progression of fibrosis and improve liver function, particularly in chronic hepatitis B.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, Miao H, et al. Progress on traditional Chinese medicine in improving hepatic fibrosis through inhibiting oxidative stress. Front Pharmacol. 2023;14:10642434.

research.title: Traditional Chinese medicine, liver fibrosis, intestinal flora: is there any connection?-a narrative review
research.description: This narrative review explores the gut-liver axis in TCM treatment of liver fibrosis. It discusses how herbal formulas may modulate intestinal microbiota to reduce endotoxemia and hepatic inflammation, providing a modern mechanistic perspective on classical spleen-dampness theories.
research.periodical: Liu Y, et al. Traditional Chinese medicine, liver fibrosis, intestinal flora: is there any connection?-a narrative review. Ann Palliat Med. 2021;10(6):6896-6906.
